ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Financial incentives to producers of Orthodox Tea 
*141.  SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA:† 
SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to provide incentives to the 
producers of Orthodox Tea to arrest falling exports and increase global Market 
share; 
(b) whether any strategy to increase India's global market share in tea has been 
evolved; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL NATH): (a) 
Government has sanctioned a scheme in  June, 2005 for grant of subsidy for 
production of orthodox tea from 1st January, 2005 to 31st March, 2007. 
(b) and (c) The strategy evolved for increasing India's global market share in 
tea includes diversification of market portfolio, value addition, marketing & 
promotion, correcting the adverse product mix of orthodox and CTC (Sant-Tea-
Curl) teas, protection of India's Intellectual Property Rights to protect its various 
brands and addressing the quality issues, etc. 
While India's global market share in tea has been coming down, the increased 
production of tea over the years has been matched by increased domestic 
consumption. In India, most of the tea manufactured is CTC 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Santosh Bagrodia. 

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2006] 
whereas internationally orthodox teas are being increasingly preferred. The 
scheme for providing financial incentives for production of orthodox tea was 
sanctioned with a view to increasing the production of orthodox teas which 
could improve India's position in international markets. 
Steps are taken to consolidate position in markets where India has a major 
share of the tea market and also to enter new markets. Market research 
projects have been commissioned in sp ecific focus markets and the reports 
have been provided to the tea industry. 
Tea Board has been taking steps to protect the various brands and has been 
successful in securing statutory recognition of Darjeeling tea in various jurisdictions 
as certification or collective marks. Darj eeling tea has also been declared as 
Geographical Indication (Gl) with effect from October 2004. 
Import duty on certain items of m achinery like tea bagging & packaging 
machinery and colour sorting machine used to improve quality and add value 
to Indian tea has been reduced to a rate of 5% presently upto May 2006. 
In order to maintain quality and retain the brand equity of Indian teas, the 
Government has issued a new Tea (Distribution and Export) Control Order, 
2005 on 01.04.2005 which prescribes strict norms for tea and stipulates that 
all teas, whether imported or exported, would be required to conform to the 
specifications cited in the new Order. 
Tea Board is also conducting promotional activities in the foreign markets and 
lending promotional support to the Indian tea exporters in their marketing efforts. 
These include participation in various fairs and exhibitions, field sampling at 
speciality stores and principal markets, media publicity, Buyer Seller Meets, 
exchange of tea delegations, etc. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I would like to say 
that since inception, I mean long time before-1961-orthodox tea production 
was 218 million Kgs. against 121 million Kgs of CTC tea, which means 64 per cent 
was orthodox. In 2003, the production of CTC increased to 717 million Kgs 
whereas orthodox went down to 87 million Kgs. In the process the percentage 
of orthodox tea is only 10 per cent. Export of orthodox tea, particularly to the 
then USSR, from South India was being

also been mentioned that they know about it that the global market share is 
going down. But saying that the market of tea is increasing in India, it has no 
reflection. The question is how do we increase global market share because it is 
going down. Sir, if you see in record terms, Sri Lanka, China, Kenya, etc. are the 
new entrants even they are increasing their share every year. 
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Please put your question. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Our export of Indian orthodox tea is going 
down. What is the Government strategy not only to re-introduce the orthodox 
tea in Russia but in the countries which have come out of USSR and find other 
markets more effectively because simple these things are not going to work. 
SHRI KAMAL NATH: Sir, the hon. Memb er is right that at a point of 
time in the 1950's the orthodox tea production was very high and has now come 
down to about 10 per cent. This is because of the Indian tea taste is much more for 
CTC tea rather than the orthodox tea. Sir, also in this, our export share has been 
going down, not only export share in all kinds of teas because of increased 
production from other countries like Kenya, Sri Lanka, etc. Sir conscious of 
this, specially for the production of green orthodox tea, a scheme was sanctioned 
on 13th June, 2005 for the period-1st January, 2005 to 31st March, 2007-which 
envisages grant of subsidy of Rs. 3 per kg for leaf grade teas and Rs. 2 per kg for 
dust grades with an additional incentive of Rs. 2 per kg for the implemental volume 
of production over the previous year. So, implementality production is also 
rewarded. This has been set up from the additional Excise Duty which, infact, 
was later withdrawn. But the fund which is collected from the additional Excise 
Duty, has been sanctioned and has been activated. Applications have been 
received. About Rs. 7.76 crores, roughly that, has been disbursed. So with the 
global taste being more for orthodox tea this mix between orthodox tea and 
the CTC variety of tea has to change. So, it is for that that orthodox tea 
production is being incentivised. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Sir, my second supplementary is this. I am 
sure the hon. Minister knows that many tea gardens in South India have been 
abandoned because the cost of production of Indian tea in the

Indian tea industry is the highest in the world. If that is so, what steps the 
Government is taking to make the Indian tea more competitive? How do you 
propose to increase productivity per hectare because this Rs. 2 or Rs. 3 subsidy

Forget about how many tea gardens are affected. This is creating havoc for 
the tea industry. 
SHRI KAMAL NATH: Sir, hon. Member is right that there is high cost of 
tea. High cost of tea is there basically for two reasons. We have the Plantation 
Labour Act. I have discussed with the West Bengal Government, I have 
discussed this with the Assam Government and with South India that we have 
very high costs. There is a social cost. One part is high cost as compared to 
other countries and the other is labour etc. At the end of the day, it is a 
relative situation. The global crisis has to be looked at relatively. The second 
is, the tea industry has not invested in the re-plantation and rejuvenation of tea 
bushes. So a large amount of our bushes  as compared to other countries are 
very old. We have proposed a Special Purpose Tea Fund and this Special 
Purpose Tea Fund includes replantation and rejuvenation fund which is going 
to be spread over 15 years. This is now is process. Yesterday in the Budget, 
the Finance Minister has sanctioned one hundred crore rupees as a rolling 
amount for this fund. This fund is Rs. 4760 crores roughly over a period of 15 
years which we propose calling a Speci al Purpose Tea Fund which is for 
replantation and rejuvenation because we have got to see that the bushes are 
young and they have a higher yield and for competitiveness, at the same time, 
we have to address the issue of high cost under the Plantation Labour Act 
which State Governments need to look at.

(a) whether it is a fact that the strength of women police in the country is not

(b) whether it is also a fact that women police in Andhra Pradesh is less

A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2006] 
Statement 
(a) Strength of women police in India was 2.5 per cent of the total police 
force as on 01-01-2005. State/UT wise details are at Statement-I (See Below) 
(b) Yes, Sir. In Andhra Pradesh the strength of women police was 1.64 per 
cent of the total police force in Andhra Pradesh as on 01-01-2005. 
(c) Police is a subject under the State List of the Constitution. However, the 
Government has been exhorting the States and Union Territories, as part of 
police reforms, to step up the recruitment of women police to at least 10 per 
cent of the total strength in a given time frame and to take effective measures 
for gender sensitization of the police force. 
The good practices in respect of gender-sensitization of police have been 
incorporated as an essential component of police training systems at the 
National Police Academy at Hyderabad, and also included in the training 
syllabus of State Police training institutions, as circulated by Bureau of Police 
Research and Development (BPR&D). These are also being disseminated 
through conferences organized by National Commission for Women and 
BPR&D.

Allocation for rural water supply scheme 
144. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Wi ll the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the amount allocated to the States under the rural water 
supply scheme during the last three years and till date, State-wise; 
(b) the details of the amount utilized by the States during this period; and 
(c) the present status of the rural water supply scheme in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) and (b) Rural drinking water is a State subject. The 
Central Government, however, supplements the efforts of the State 
Governments in providing drinking water facilities in rural habitations by 
30 

[1 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
rendering financial assistance under a Centrally sponsored scheme namely 
Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP). The State-wise details 
of the amount allocated, releases made and expenditure reported by the States 
during the last three years and in the cu rrent year are at Statements I to IV. 
(See below) 
(c) Rural Drinking Water is one of the components of Bharat Nirman, which 
has been conceived as a plan to build rural infrastructure in a 4-year period-2005-06 
to 2008-09. The plan of the Government under Bharat Nirman for rural drinking water 
supply is to fully covery 55,067 uncovered habitations. In addition, habitations, 
which have slipped back from full coverage to partial coverage due to failure 
of systems or sources, and habitations, which have quality problems, will also 
be covered. During the current year (2005-06), 54,890 rural habitations are 
reported to have been covered till 31st January, 2006 which include 
uncovered, slipped back and quality affected habitations, as against the annual 
target of 56,270 rural habitations. 
Upto 20% of the Annual ARWSP funds may be allocated for Swajaldhara 
scheme. These funds are allocated to the States every year. The States then make 
district wise allocation and inform the Department of Drinking Water Supply, 
which releases the instalments accordingly. 
To institutionalize community based water quality monitoring and 
surveillance system in the country, Government of India has introduced the 
National Rural Drinking Water Quality Monitoring and Surveillance 
Programme in February 2006. The total estimated Government of India share 
for this programme for the remaining 10th Five Year Plan period would be Rs. 
269.88 crores. An amount of Rs. 57.84 crore has been released to the States 
during the current financial year for implementation of the programme. 
For capacity building of various stakeholders working in water supply and 
sanitation sectors as well as for crea ting awareness amongst the people on 
these issues, Communication and Capacity Development Units (CCDU) have 
been sanctioned in 23 States so far with an outlay of Rs. 23.82 crore.

Rural development and infrastructure creation 
*145. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the amount spent by Government during the last two years for each 
scheme of rural development, State-wise; 
(b) whether Government have any proposal to spend at least Rs. 1 lakh crores 
in the coming year on rural development and creation of infrastructure; 
(d) the amount allocation for each scheme, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) to (d) The Ministry of Rural Development implements at 
present through State Governments major rural development schemes like the 
Swarnjayanti Garm Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY), Sampooma Grameen Rozgar 
Yojana (IAY), Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana 
36 

[1 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(PMGSY), Watershed Development Programme viz, Integrated Wastelands 
Development Programme (IWDP), Drought Prone Areas Programme (DPAP) 
and Desert Development Programme (DDP), Accelerated Rural Water Supply 
Programme (ARWSP), Swajaldhara and the Central Rural Sanitation 
Programme (CRSP)/Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC). 
2. Scheme and State-wise funds released by the Central Government in the 
last two years (2003-04 and 2004-05) are given at Statement I to III. (see below). 
3. All schemes mentioned above are meant for rural development and 
creation of infrastructure. Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) is 
meant for rural connectivity, Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY) is meant for 
providing houses to the rural poor and Rural Water Supply Programme is for 
providing drinking water. However, need based sustainable rural 
infrastructure is also created under SGRY, NFFWP and SGSY. The National 
Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA) has been passed by Parliament and 
is being implemented in 200 districts in the first phase. Besides, giving 
guarantee of 100 days of employment to rural poor, this Act w ill also create 
rural infrastructure. The Ministry of Rural Development in consultation with the 
Planning Commission has also launched a pilot phase for the implementation of 
the Provision of Urban Amenities in Rural Areas (PURA) Scheme which provides 
for rural infrastructure. Investment by other Ministries like Surface Transport, 
Telecommunication, Human Resource Development, etc. also results in rural 
development and creation of infrastructure. 
4. The Finance Minister in his Budget Speech 2005-06 has announced the 
Bharat Nirman Programme which is a four year business plan for 
development of rural infrastructure with a total estimated investment of Rs. 
1,74,000 crores. The components of rural infrastrucutre identified under the 
programme are irrigation, rural drinking water, rural roads, rural housing, rural 
electrification and rural telephone connectivity. In the Union Budget of 2006-07, a 
provision of Rs. 31443.62 crore is proposed for the Ministry of Rural 
Development for plan schemes. 
5. Scheme-wise and State-wise allocations for the coming year depend on the 
Budgetary allocations and are based on scheme-wise criteria for inter-state 
allocation.

Growth rate of industrial production 
*146. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the annual growth rate of industrial production is 
expected to increase in the current year as compared to the last three years; 
(b) if so, the actual growth-rate duri ng the last three years and the 
estimated growth rate for the year 2005-06; 
(c) whether Government have also identified those industries in which 
growth rate is either increasing or decr easing, as compared to the last three 
years; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL 
NATH): (a) and (b) The annual growth of industrial production, in terms of GDP 
(at constant 1999-2000 prices) originating from mining & quarrying, 
manufacturing, electricity, gas & water supply, and construction for the current 
year 2005-06 stands at 9% as" per the Advance Estimate of the Central 
Statistical Organisation, compared to 8.6% in 2004-05, 7.6% in 2003-04 and 
7% in 2002-03. 
(c) and (d) The industries whose growth rates increased during the period 
2002-03 to 2004-05 are Beverages & Tobacco products, Cotton textiles, Jute 
products, Textile products, Machinery & equipment other Manufacturing 
industries, Chemicals, Leather & its products, and Metal products & parts. 
Also, electricity showed a marginal increase. 
The industries currently showing a decreasing growth rate are Food 
products, Wool, Silk & man-made fibres, Wood & its products, Paper and its 
products, Rubber, Plastic, Petroleum & coal products, Non-metallic mineral 
products, Basic metals & alloy and Transport equipment & parts. Mining also 
registered a decline.

Priority to Indian farmers' interests in WTO negotiations 
   864. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE:                
SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the interest of farmers be kept in mind while negotiating in the 
second round of WTO negotiations since in India million of farmers depend 
on agriculture; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the devel oped countries were requested to cut 
their trade distorting agriculture subsidies by 83 percent and if so, what was 
their reaction; 
(c) what action Government propose to take to safeguard the interests of the 
farmers; and 
(d) whether provisions will be made to safeguard food and livehood 
securities and rural development? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Towards fulfillment of the objective of the G-20, of which India is a 
founder Member, to bring down the levels of applied trade-distorting domestic support 
provided to their farm sector by developed countries, the G-20 has proposed 80% 
cuts in the overall trade-distorting domestic support by the highest subsidizer, 
namely, the European Union (EU) Member States, with the United States (US) 
and Japan attracting cuts of 75%. The EU, in turn, has proposed that it can accept 
cuts of 70% provided, inter alia, US and Japan agree to cut their support by 60%. 
The US has similarly proposed 60% cuts for itself and for Japan, provided, inter 
alia, the EU is agreeable to a cut of 83%. At the Sixth Ministerial Conference 
of the WTO held between 13-18 December 2005 at Hong Kong, a declaration was 
adopted at its conclusion, whose key outcome in this respect is that in a three-
band structure for reducing trade-distorting domestic support, the Member with the 
highest level of permitted support (EU) will be in the top band with the highest 
cuts, the two Members with second and third highest levels of support (Japan and 
US) will be in the second band, and a ll other developed countries and such 
developing countries that have entitlement to provide Aggregate Measurement of 
Support (AMS) will be in the lowest band with 
54 

[1 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
the smallest cuts. Furthermore, discip lines will be developed to achieve 
effective cuts in trade-distorting domestic support. The negotiations are 
proceeding with a view to establish modalities in agriculture by 30 April 2006, 
with draft Schedules to be submitted by July 31, 2006, under an overall resolve 
by WTO Ministers at Hong Kong to complete the Doha Work Programme 
fully and conclude negotiations in 2006. 
(c) and (d) India's overall objectives in the negotiations launched at the Doha 
Ministerial Conference of the WTO in November 2001 have been to secure a final 
outcome on agriculture that is consistent with the agreed negotiating mandate 
for early elimination of all forms of export subsidies, substantial and effective 
reductions in trade-distorting domestic support, and substantial improvements in 
market access particularly for products of export interest to developing 
countries. Simultaneously, it has been agreed that special and differential 
treatment for developing countries will be integral to all aspects of the 
negotiations, recognizing that agriculture is of critical importance to the economic 
development of developing country Members and they must be able to pursue 
agricultural policies that are supportive of their development goals, poverty 
reduction strategies, food security and livelihood concerns. 
The Hong Kong Minister ial Declaration also in cluded a decision to 
eliminate export subsidies, which are mainly provided by some developed 
countries, by 2013, with substantial part in the first half of implementation period 
and to eliminate cotton export subsidies by developed countries by 2006. 
Developing countries will continue to benefit from the provisions on marketing 
and transport subsidies on agricultural exports for five years after the end date 
for elimation of all forms of export subsidies. On trade-distorting domestic 
support, the three heaviest subsidizers will attract the steepest cuts also in the 
reductions in their AMS, and trade-distorting domestic subsidies provided to 
cotton are to be reduced more ambitiously and over a shorter period of time. 
Developing countries like India, with no AMS, will be exempt from any cuts on 
de minimis and on overall trade-distorting suport levels. In respect of market 
access commitments it has been agreed that a four-band tariff reduction formula 
will be developed. In order to address their f ood security, livelihood and rural 
development needs, developing countries to have the flexibility to self-designate an 
appropriate number of Special Products, whose treastment will be more 
flexible. In order to safeguard farmers in developing countries against import 
surges 
55 

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2006] 
and adverse global price movements, im port quantity and price triggers have 
been agreed as the core structural elements of the Special Safeguard Mechanism. 
The Government has been holding stakeholder consultations to protect and 
pursue our national interest, interests of the farmers and exporters. Government 
is committed to safeguard food and livelihood security and rural development 
needs of India's agricultural sector and to achieve its development imperatives in 
line with the Doha mandate and subsequent decisions contained in the General 
Council Decision of August 1, 2004 and the Hong Kong Ministerial 
Declaration to protect the intersts of  all domestic stakeholdes, especially, 
farmers and exporters.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INSUSTRY(SHRI ASHWANI KUMAR): (a) (b), and (d) During the hearing of a 
Civil Writ Petition praying to direct the Government of India to facilitate 
revocation of a patent granted by European Patent Office on a soft-milling wheat, 
the Hon'ble Supreme Court had directed*the appointment of a Committee to 
examine the matter. Accordingly, a Committee was appointed by Secretary, 
Department of Agricultural Research & Education and Director General, Indian 
Council of Agricultural Research. The report of the Committee has since been

(c) Patents are sought and obtained by applicants/inventor, both Indian and 
foreign, in different countries to safeguard and promote their commercial and other 
interest. Such patents are granted under the sovereign prerogative of c ountries 
according to their respective patent laws and have territorial * effect, that is, they 
are effective only in the country of grant. In order to qualify for grant of patent in 
any country an invention, whether process or product, has to meet the criteria of 
patentability, namely, novelty, inventiveness and industrial applicability. Indian 
goods/items, which are already in public knowledge/domain, cannot be patented. 
As patents are essentially private righ ts they are normally challenged, in 
accordance with the patent laws of the country concerned, by the person(s) 
whose interests are affected/jeopardized. 
64 

[1 March. 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
As and when information is received about patent being obtained on certain 
items which are not considered patentable and which affect Indian interests, steps 
are taken to assess whether the grant of such patent can be challenged under the 
patent laws of the country concerned. Earlier a patent granted in the United 
States of America on he use of turmeric in wound healing was successfully 
challenged and was also cancalled by the "Patent Office of the country 
concerned. Similarly, a patent on the fungicidal property of Neem, granted in 
Europe, was successfully challgend. Th e claims of the patent on Basmati 
Ricelines and grains granted in the United States of America which had the 
potential of affecting India's commercial interest were also challenged. The said 
claims were subsiquently cancelled by the United States Patent and Trademark 
Office and the title of the patent was also amended. 
In order to provide better protection to goods bearing geographical 
indications, the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and 
Protection) Act, 1999 was enacted. This law provides for protection through 
registration of geographical indications. The registration of a geographical 
indication shall, if valid, give to the authorized user the exclusive right to the use of 
the geographical indication in relation to the goods in respect of which the 
geographical indication is registered. It also gives the registered proprietor and the 
authorized user the right to obtain relief in respect of infringement of the 
geographical indication. The Act was brought into force with effect from 15th 
September, 2003. This being a new legislation, steps have been taken to organize 
awareness programmes throughout India in a phased manner, and thereby to 
promote registration of Indian geographical indications. Fiften sensitization 
workshops were conducted during 2003-04 and 2004-05. As a result of these 
intiatives, the Geographical Indications Registry has been able to receive 46 
applications for registration of geographical indications upto 31st December 
2005, out of which 27 have already been regsitered. The registered goods bearing 
geographical indications, inter alia, include Darjeeling tea, Chanderi Sari, 
Pochampalli Ikat, Kota Doria, Kangra Tea, Coorg Orange, Channapatna toys and 
dolls, Nanjanagud Banana, Mysore Agarbathi, etc.

Export of Chinese articles to India through Nepal 
896. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will th e Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Nepal tops in garment export to India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Indian markets provide a duty free access for all Nepalese 
manufactured articles; 
(d) whether Chinese products are also finding their way to India through Nepal 
and enjoying the above privilege; and 
(e) if so, the action plan of Government to impose safeguards against Chinese 
products entering our markets through Nepal? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir, the imports of 
readymade garments from Nepal were Rs. 29.13 crores during 2004-05 as per 
Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics Data. 
(c) For duty free access into India, the Nepalese goods should have been 
made wholly from Indian/Nepalese materials, or the Nepalese goods have 
undergone a 4-digit level change of the Harmonized commodities Description and 
Coding system. Besides, third country inputs in the goods manufactured in Nepal 
should not exceed 75% of the ex-factory price during the first year, from 6.3.2002 
to 5.3.2003 and 70% thereafter. Further, duty free imports from Nepal into India in 
respect of four items viz., vanaspati, 
81 

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2006] 
copper products, acrylic yarn and zinc oxides have been restricted to annual quotas. 
(d) and (e) The India-Nepal Treaty of Trade prohibits export of third country goods 
from Nepal into India without the fulfilment of value addition and processing conditions 
prescribed under the Treaty. Hence, Chinese goods cannot be re-exported from Nepal into 
India under the India-Nepal Treaty of Trade. Government of India makes all efforts to 
prevent and control smuggling across the India-Nepal border. In addition, under the 
India-Nepal Agreement to Control Unauthorised Trade, Governments of the two 
countries cooperate with each other to prevent unauthorized trade across their border. 
Field formations of Directorate of Revenue Intelligence have also been sensitised to 
prevent smuggling of third country products through Nepal.

December 2005;

that shows growth in export and the total exports during the above period, item-
wise, month-wise, category-wise; and

above? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND

December, 2005 is increased availability  from other regions in respect of 
chilly, low intake of fresh ginger by Pakistan, low unit value realisation in 
respect of turmeric, higher prices as compared to other major competitors in 
respect of seed spices, and low unit value realisation of vanilla exported from 
India. 
The steps taken to improve the export of spices are as under: 
 Promoting worldwide direct sale of premium category of branded Indian 
spices viz., "Flavourit", since March 2005. 
 Promotion of export of organic spices. 
 Upgradation of technology for high-end value-addition and 
developing capabilities to meet the emerging global food safety 
standards. 
 Adoption of high-tech processing technologies such as cryo-
grinding steam sterilisation, super fluid extraction and advanced 
system of packaging.

exporters for testing among other things, pesticide residues, aflatoxin, 
physical, chemical and microbial  contaminants and chemical 
composition of spices. 
 Adoption of quality certifica tion procedures leading to accreditation 
under ISO, HACCP, SQF 2000, organic certification etc.

902. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) how SAFTA will lead to a rise in inter-regional trade; 
(b) whether it is a fact that Pakistan has still not adopted the SAFTA; 
(c) with the beginning of SAFTA, how India's trade would grow from the 
present Rs. 25000 crores with SAARC; and 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2006] 
(d) what could be the main areas of cooperation between the SAARC 
countries after the emergence of SAFTA? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) In terms of phased tariff 
liberalization programme under Rule 7 of the Agreement on South Asian Free 
Trade Area (SAFTA), in two years, Non-Least Developed Contracting States 
(NLDCs) will bring down tariffs to 20% , while Least Developed Contracting 
States (LDCs) wil bring them down to 30%. Non-LDCs will then bring down 
tariffs from 20% to 0-5% in 5 years (Sri Lanka 6 years), while LDCs will do so 
in 8 years. This tariff liberalization programme would not be applicable to the 
items kept in the Sensitive List by each Member State. All the Member States 
of SAFTA are scheduled to effect tariff liberalization with effect from 1st July, 
2006, except Nepal which would effect it from 1st August 2006, subject to the 
condition that the tariff liberalization programme for the first two years would 
be completed by 31st December, 2007. After SAFTA becomes operational 
from 1st July 2006 the intra-regional  SAARC trade is expected to grow 
significantly, but the same cannot be quantified at this stage. 
(b) The SAARC Secretariat has intim ated that the Government of 
Pakistan has ratified the SAFTA. 
(c) After the tariff liberalization programme of SAFTA comes into force from 
1st July, 2006, India's trade with SAARC countries is expected to grow 
substantially, but at this stage it cannot be quantified. 
(d) Article 3 of the SAFTA Agreement sets out objectives and principles 
which, inter alia, provides for eliminating barriers to trade, cross- border 
movement of goods between the Contracting States, creating effective 
mechanism for implementation of the Agreement and establishing a frame work 
for further regional cooperation to expand and enhance the mutual benefits of 
this Agreement. Article 10 of the Agreement prescribes the institutional 
Arrangements for the administration and implementation of the Agreement.

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2006] 
(c) whether it has come to Government's notice that Pak intruders have started 
coming through Bangladesh/Nepal borders; and 
(d) if so, the action being taken by Government to stop this menace? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI SHRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) As per existing Visa Regime, Pak 
nationals are not granted "T ourist Visa'. They are gr anted 'Visitor Visa', for 
meeting relatives/friends or any other legitimate purpose. As per available 
information, 2,392 such Pak nationals who came to India are missing as on 
30.11.2005.

foreigners staying illegally in the country.

its agents for subversive activity and espionage through the porous Indo-
Bangladesh and Indo-Nepal Borders.

been taken by the Government which include strengthening of Border Security 
Force (BSF) by providing them with modern equipments and surveillance 
gadgets; raising of additional battalions  of BSF; reduction of gaps between 
border outposts; intensification of pa troliing and accelerated programme of 
construction of border roads and border fencing. As regards indo-Nepal border, it is 
guarded by Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB); which is getting strengthened by new 
raising and induction of modern equipments and surveillance gadgets. Further, 
State policing infrastructure in the border districts on Indo-Nepal Border has been 
strengthened by providing special assistance under the Modernization of Police 
Forces Scheme.

Accelerated Rural Water Supply Progr amme (ARWSP) for Drinking Water

†980. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of LABOUR AND

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI CHANDRA SEKHAR  SAHU): (a) and (b) The 
Government has made assessment of incidence of poverty for the population as a 
whole. According to the NSSO survey (1999-2000), about 26% of the population 
is living Below Poverty Line. Rural economic being agricultural based, a large 
number of agricultral labourers live below the poverty line. However, no estimate 
of poverty among agricultural workers separately is available. 
(c) and (d) Under the provisions of Minimum Wages Act, 1948, both 
Central and State Governments are the appropriate Governments to fix and 
revise minimum wages in the scheduled employments under their respective 
jurisdictions. According to the Act, the appropriate Governments review/revise the 
minimum wages in the scheduled employments under their respective 
jurisdictions at an interval not exceeding five years. In certain cases minimum 
wages include variable dearness allowance (VDA), which is reviewed/revised 
periodically twice a year effective April and October. A statement indicating the 
rates of minimum wages for agricultlral workers by different Governments both in 
State and Central spheres is at Statement. (See below). The wages of agricultural 
workers do not directly

995. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: W ill the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the genesis and objective of Indira Awaas Yojana and how does it 
differ from other schemes for dwelling construction; 
(b) what are the criteria for allocation of funds under IAY to States; 
(c) the funds allowed to Rajasthan, under IAY, during 2004-05 and 2005-2006 
and targets fixed thereof, year-wise; 
183

Yojana during said period, against the target fixed; 
(e) whether any proposals from the State Government are still pending 
consideration with the centre; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) and (b) The genesis of 
the Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY) can be  traced to the programmes of rural 
employment, which began in the early 1980s. Construction of houses was one of 
the major activities under the National Rural Employment Programme (NREP), 
launched in 1980, and the Rural Landless Employment Guarantee Programme 
(RLEGP), started in 1983. There was, however, no uniform policy for rural 
housing in the States. As per the announcement made by the Government of 
India in June 1985, a part of the RLEGP funds was earmarked for the 
construction of houses for Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes and freed bonded 
labourers. As a result, the Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY) was launched during 1985-
86 as a sub-scheme of the RLEGP. The IAY thereafter continued as a sub-scheme 
of the Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) since its launching in April, 1989. 6% of 
the total JRY funds was allocated for implementation of the IAY. From the year 
1993-94, the scope of the IAY was extended to cover below the poverty line Non 
Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes families in the rural areas. Simultaneously, 
the allocation of funds for implementing the scheme was raised from 6% to 
10% of the total resources available under the JRY at the national level, subject 
to the condition that the funds going to SC/ST poor should not be less than 6% of 
the total JRY allocation. The IAY was de-linked from the JRY and made an 
independent scheme with effect from 1 st January 1996. Now out of the total 
allocation, a minimum of 60% has to be spent on SC/ ST BPL families. 
Expenditure under the Scheme on other eligible BPL families cannot exceed 
40%. Presently, the IAY is implemented in all the States/UTs except Delhi and 
Chandigarh with the objective to primarily help construction of dwelling units 
by members of Scheduled Castes/ Scheduled Tribes, freed bonded labourers and 
also below the proverty line non-SC/ST rural households by providing them 
financial assistance in the form of grant-in-aid. The expenditure of the scheme 
is shared between Centre and Stat e in the ratio of 75:25. Under the 
Programme minimum 60% of the funds are earmarked for SC/ST BPL families 
and upto 40% for the non SC/ST BPL families. With a view to target housing 
shortage in a 
184

for fund allocation has been modified to assign 75% weightage to housing 
shortage and 25% weightage to poverty ratio for State level allocation of the 
Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY) funds as against the 50:50 weightage given to the 
two variables earlier.

Implementation of centrally funded programmes 
1002. SHRI T.T.V. DHINKARAN: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of centrally funded programmes being implemented in the 
country; 
(b) the details of backward districts/regions identified for special 
developmental care; and 
(c) the steps taken to improve the backward districts in the country 
including the use of advanced technology? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) The Ministry of 
Rural Development implements through the State Governments a number of 
schemes namely, the Swranjayati Gram Swarojgar Yojana (SGSY) for self 
employment, the Sampoorna Gramin Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) and the 
National Food for Work Programme (NFFWP) as wage employment, the Indira 
Awaas Yojana (IAY) for providing shelter, Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana 
(PMGSY) for rural connectivity, Drought Prone Areas Programme (DPAP), 
Desert Development Programme (DDP), Integrated Wastelands Development 
Projects (IWDP) for Area Development through Watersheds Projects, the 
Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP), the Swajaldhara for 
providing safe drinking water and the Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC) for 
Sanitation Programmes. The National Rural Employment Gurantee Act 
(NREGA) has come into force in the id entified 200 most backward districts 
that provide legal guarantee of 100 days of unskilled manual work to each 
rural household demanding for it in a financial year. 
(b) A Statement showing 200 backward districts identifed for first phase of 
implementation under NREGA for special developmental care is given at 
Statement. (See Below) 
(c) The Ministry of Rural Development is providing adequate resources to 
these districts through implementation of various schemes meant for self, wage 
employment, housing, area development and basic minimum services like 
drinking water in rural areas.

Recommendations of Inter-Ministerial Group on SGSY 
1004. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the steps taken by Government in implementing Inter-Ministerial 
Group recommendations for launching pilot Programme under Swaranjayanti 
Gram Swarozgar Yojana for unemployed youths in rural areas for 2005-07; 
(b) the Name of districts in the State of Andhra Pradesh selected for 
launching the programme in the 1 st and 2nd phase; and 
(c) the amount allocated for the Project for the year 2005-06? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) to (c) An Inter-
Ministerial Group (IMG) had recommended that a demand-driven skill 
development programme may be designed to equip the unemployed rural 
youths from the below Poverty Line (BPL) households with marketable skills 
which would enable them to either secure placement in the organized 
establishments or secure sustainable self- 
208 

[1 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
employment through micro enterprise. Subsequentjo the recommendations of 
IMG, the Government decided to launch a pilot programme for skill 
development under Swaranjayanti Gram Swarojgar Yojana (SGSY) for the 
unemployed youths from BPL families in the rural areas. The guidelines of 
the pilot scheme has been issued and circulated to the States. 
(b) During the pilot phase of the scheme (2005-2007) it is proposed to -cover 
at least 1000-2000 rural youth per year in 100 selected districts. These pilot 
projects would be funded as Special Projects under SGSY, with the same 
pattern of assistance (75.25) applied mutatis mutandis to the training programme. 
So far no such special projects have been received from the State Governments.

Setting up of sericulture enterprises in Orissa 
1011. MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in order to generate employment opportunities in the 
backward Orissa, the State Government proposes to set up sericulture 
enterprises in the most backward KBK regions; 
(b) whether this project is being implemented with financial help from 
Central Silk Board; 
(c) if so, the progress so far made in execution of the project; and 
(d) what is the action plan of the Centre to help this cash-strapped State in 
silk worm rearing with a view to provide employment to rural masses? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Both the Central Silk Board 
(CSB) and the State Government of Orissa have been implementing following 
projects in different districts of Orissa including the KBK region to provide 
gainful employment opportunities to sericulturists; 
1. Catalytic Development Programme (CDP) in different sericultural areas 
of Orissa including KBK districts; 
2. Tasar Eco Race Development Project in Similipal Biosphere of 
Mayurbhanj district. 
(c) CSB has been implementing various schemes/components under the 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme viz. "Catalytic Development Programme" in 
collaboration with various state sericulture departments including Orissa state 
for promotion of silk industry in the country, during Tenth Plan. The 
components under the CDP envisage development and expansion of host 
plantation, development of farm infrastructure, upgradation of reeling and 
processing technologies in silk, enterprise development programme etc. CSB 
has spent/released Rs. 50.62 lakhs, Rs. 82.29 lakhs, Rs. 24.32 lakhs and Rs. 
120.89 lakhs respectively during 2002-03, 2003-04, 2004-05 and 2005-06 (upto 
January, 2006). The CDP has been under implementation in different 
districts of Orissa State including KBK districts. 
219 

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2006] 
A Modal Tasar Eco Race Development Project is being implemented in 
Mayurbhanj district at a total cost Rs. 2.60 crores which included CSB's share 
of Rs. 39.13 lakh. CSB has so far released Rs. 34.23 lakhs mainly towards 
purchase of seed cocoons, transportation, establishment of base unit and 
organization of camps in the project areas. The project has helped to conserve 
the modal eco race population and supported the local rearers to harvest 
quality tasar cocoons without disturbing the forest ecology. 
(d) The CSB would continue these shemes/projects in collaboration with 
the State Government to cover more beneficiaries. The CSB has formulated a 
Special Swarnajayanti Gram Swarojag ar Yojana (SGSY) Project for the 
development of tasar culture in the state at a total cost of Rs. 11.36 crores and 
submitted the proposal to the Ministry of Rural Development for financial 
assistance. The project would be implemented over a period of five years between 
2006 and 2010. The project envisages to produce 70.14 MT tasar silk and 29.91 
MT of eri spun silk through 3220 beneficiaries.

Statement 
Measures taken by the Government in the recent past to help the textile 
sector 
  ♦ To improve productivity and quality of cotton for manufacture and 
export of competitive downstream textile products, Government has 
launched the Technology Mission on Cotton (TMC). The Mission has 
achieved success in increasing the productivity and reducing the 
contamination through upgradation of cotton market yards and 
modernisation of Ginning and Pressing factories. 
222 

[1 March, 2006} RAJYA SABHA 
♦   The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS)  was 
launched to facilitate the modernisation and upgradation of the textile 
industry both in the organised and unorganized sector. The Scheme 
has been further fine taned to increase the rapid investments in the 
targeted sub-sectors of the textile industry. The cost of machinery has 
been further brought down by reducing the customs duty on imports. 
♦ For speedy modernisation of the textile processing sector, 
Government has introduced w.e.f. 20-04-05, a credit linked capital 
subsidy @10% under TUFS, in addition to the existing 5% interest 
reimbursement. 
♦ For small scale textile and jute industrial units, Government has 
enhanced, the rate of Credit Linked Capital Subsidy (CLCS) from 12% 
to 15% w.e.f. 13-01-05. 
♦ In order to facilitate modernisation of the Powerloom Sector, 
Schemes such as High-tech Weaving Parks, Modernisation and 
Strengthening of Powerloom Service Centres, Group Workshed 
Scheme and Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme @20% have 
been introduced. Also, the Government has enhanced, w.e.f. 13-01-05, 
the capital ceiling for machinery from Rs. 60.00 lakh to Rs. 100.00 lakh 
under 20% capital subsidy scheme-TUFS. 
♦ To provide the textile industry with world-class infrastructure 
facilities for setting up their textile units meeting international 
environmental and social standards, a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) 
based Scheme known as the "Scheme for Integrated Textile Park 
(SITP)" has been introduced in July 2005. 
♦ In 2004-05 Budget, the entire textile sector, except for man-made 
fibre and filament yarn was provided optional exemption from excise 
duty. In 2005-06 Budget, Central Value-aided Tax (CENVAT) on 
Polyester Filament Yarn has been reduced from 24% to 16%. These 
modifications in fiscal levies aim at attracting more investments for 
modernization of textile sector. 
♦ To facilitate import of state of the art machinery to make our products 
internationally competitive in post quota regime, in 2005-06 
223 

RAJYA SABHA [1 March, 2006] 
Budget, the customs duty on textile machinery has been brought down 
to 10% except 23 machinery appearing in List 49 which attracts 
Basic Customs Duty (BCD) of 15%. The concessional duty of 5% 
continues to be at 5% on most of the machinery items. 
♦ In 2005-06 Budget, 30 items of knitting and knitwear have been de-
reserved. This would facilitate setting up of large sized 
modernized units for meeting the international competition. 
♦ Government has launched the Debt Restructuring Scheme w.e.f. Sept., 
2003 with the principal objective to permit banles to lend to the 
textile sector at 8-9% rate of interest. 
♦ In order to cater to the growin g skilled manpower requirements at 
shop floor level, Government is providing assistance for 
strengthening existing and opening new Apparel Training and Design 
Centres (ATDCs). 
♦ Government has allowed 100% Foreign Direct Investment in the textile 
sector under automatic route. 
♦ Government has dereserved the readymade garments, hosiery and 
knitwear from SSI sector so that  large scale investments may be 
encouraged in these sectors. 
•:• National Institute of Fashion Technology (NIFT) has been set up to 
provide the leadership role in sensitizing the Industry to the concept of 
value addition by inducting trained professionals to manage the industry. 
This has resulted in an increased demand for trained professionals in 
various sectors servicing the industry. 
♦ To take a serious look at Fashion Education in the changing 
business context of the opening up of World Economies, 
Government is taking steps for:—

♦ Establishing an institution of National excellence for imparting 
Fashion Business Education with International Benchmarking. 
♦ Appointing a nodal agency for standardizing and benchmarking 
Fashion Business Education in the country. 
♦ Setting up an Apex Body to train the teachers/trainers imparting 
Fashion Business Education in the country.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) Yes, Sir. An assessment of the status of export of 
handicrafts was undertaken recently through Export Promotion Council for 
Handicrafts (EPCH). 
(b) The outcome of the assessment is as under: 
(i) The export of handicrafts is growing at an average annual growth rate of 
15%. 
(ii) The major contributors to exports are: Embroidered and Crocheted goods 
(32.46)%; Art-Metal-ware (31.90%), shawls as Artware (28.45%) 
and Imitation Jewellery (28.41 %).

Eastern Region including NER (6.33%), Western Region (5.66%) and 
Southern Region (4.99%), and the target and export figures of Handicrafts are 
prescribed and maintained for the country as a whole and no State-wise targets 
are fixed.

Promotion, Special Handicrafts Training Project for skill upgradation, Credit

[1 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN (Kerala): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I support 
this Bill which would give more chances to the minorities in higher education. 
However, I have my apprehensions about this Bill, if the provisions of this Bill 
are implemented without caution. The Bill has been closely scrutinised by the 
Standing Committee. In its Report the Committee has emphasised and I 
quote: 
'The Committee feels that the Bill must provide adequate safeguards for 
preventing the misuse of the minority status by an institution." 
This apprehension was mentioned in the Standing Committee Report. I am 
not supporting the viewpoints raised by my BJP colleagues in this House. 
Sir, the minority communities, especially, the Muslim community, are lagging 
behind socially, economically and educationally. The minorities in this country 
are suffering from mental agony because of the hardcore Hindutva line pursued 
by the previous Government. Fortunately, due to the initiative taken by the 
majority in the country, by the secular-minded people in our country, now the 
minority communities have the added confidence to live as citizens of this 
country. In that direction this Bill will help the minority to gain more confidence. 
At the same time, Sir, I would like to mention that whenever we passed this kind 
of a legislation, we had certain bitter ex periences. There is every possibility of 
misusing the scope of this Bill. There are richer sections in our society. As per 
the Bill, an individual from a minority community can start a minority institution. If 
he has the money to purchase the land and construct the building, he can go 
ahead and start a minority institution. So, utmost caution should be taken in 
this regard. This right to start a minority educational institution should not be 
reserved only for the economically privileged minority among the minorities. 
That is the issue. The Government should give an assurance to this House that 
the benefit would not go to the rich mi nority, the so called economic minority 
among the minorities. So, utmost caution should be taken to avoid its misuse 
while implementing this bill. Any indi vidual can go and say that he is from a 
minority community. That is the problem. This is my apprehension so far as this 
Bill is concerned. Similarly, we have the experience of Kerala. Shri A.K. Antony is 
the hon. Member of this House. The Government of Kerala gave permission to 
start unaided colleges and a majority of them

DR. RADHAKANT NAYAK (Orissa): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I am thankful to you for having

don't want to discuss some procedural matters which perhaps are engaging the attention of the 
House. I would concentrate on certain substantial issues that concern this Bill, and support it. 
Sir, most of the issues that have arisen and discussed by the Opposition relate to Article 
30 of the Indian Constitution. Sir, this article has been debated in extenso in the Constituent 
Assembly debates; and most of the issues, most of the apprehensions that have been raised 
today also, have been discussed there and, thereafter, the Article has been adopted. This article 
has also been tested, from time to time, not only by different

Constitution which now, more or less, is not being agreed to by the 
Opposition. Sir, the implementation of this Article is a mandate given to all the 
Governments which are being democratically elected in this country. Sir, therefore, 
instead of procedures, I would go into the substance of this Article. 
Sir, the first thing this Article enjoins on the Government is the protection of 
minorities. Sir, the phenom enon of minorities is not limited to this country 
alone. One of the Members of the Opposition has said that in no other 
Constitution, in no other country such a pr otective provision is found. It is not 
correct. 
A reference was made to Canada for example, Sir, Canada is like us, a multi-
ethnic country and there the Catholics ar e considered in some parts of the 
French-Quebec as minorities. In many ot her countries, such kind of situation 
exists and the law also exists for the protection of the minorities. I would not 
take long to discuss the various naunces of this Article, nor other provisions in 
the Constition. But I would read it out to you as a reminder to this august House 
an extract from, one of the most important landmark judgements of the Supreme 
Court viz the T.M.A. Pai Foundation Vs. the State of Karnataka. Now, Sir, I will read 
out to you the judgement. I will take only 3-4 minutes. I quote, "Our country is 
often depicted as a person in the form of 'Bharat Mata, Mother India'. The people of 
India are regarded as her children with their welfare being in her heart. Like any 
loving mother, the welfare of the family is of paramount importance for her. For a 
healthy family, it is important that each member is strong and healthy." 
Unquote Sir, this is an eleven-member judgement of the Supreme Court which, 
quote. Then, "But then, all members do not have the same constition, whether 
physical and/or mental. For harmonious and healthy growth, it is but natural 
for the parents, and the mother in particular, to give more attention and food to 
the weaker child so as to help him/her become stronger. Giving extra food and 
attention and ensuring private tution to help in his/her studies will, in a sense, 
amount to giving the weaker child preferential treatment." Un quote Somebody 
said of reverse discrimination, which it is not. It is a positive treatment; it's a 
preferential treatment. I quote again, "Just as lending physical support to the 
aged and the infirm, or providing a special diet, cannot be regarded as

unfair or unjust, similarly, conferring certain rights on a special class, for good

minorities because of their numerical handicap and to instil in them a sense of 
security and confidence, even through the minorities cannot be perse regarded as 
weaker sections or underprivileged segments of the society," Sir, I will continue,

that go into the making of a map. Each person, whatever his/her language, 
caste, religion has his/her individual identity, which has to be preserved, so that 
when pieced together it goes to form a depiction with the different geographical 
features of India. These small pieces of marble, in the form of human beings, which 
may individually be dissimilar to each other, when placed together in a systematic 
manner, produce the beautiful map of India. Each piece, like a citizen of India, plays

insignificant stone, but when placed in a proper manner, goes into the making of a

passing the Bill, the Government has again come forward with an Ordinance, and 
subsequent to the Ordinance, this Bill has been brought in before the House. First of all, I

last 12 or 13 months as far as the implementation of the National Commission for Minority

affiliated to a particular university, and what experience has been gathered by the 
Government during the last 12 months of the implementation of the National

original Act, in the National

SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR (Assam): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, thank you for

Institutions (Amendment) Bill, 2005. I support this Bill. At the same time, I congratulate the

and economic conditions of minorities. The National Commission for Minority 
Educational Institutions (Amendment) Bill also seeks to plug loopholes, which hindered 
the functioning of the Commission since its inception in 2004. It proposes to relax the 
provision, which restricted minority institutions seek affiliation to any of the six listed 
scheduled universities, that is, Delhi Un iversity, North-Eastern Hill University,

the NOC.

Constitution (Ninety-Third) Amendment Bill, 2005. According to this Amendment, "The 
State can, by law, make special provision for the advancement of any socially and 
educationally backward classes of citizens or for the Scheduled Castes or the Scheduled 
Tribes in so far as

Female Foeticide in the Country 
DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA(Rajasthan): Successive census reports have 
highlighted India's skewed sex ratio, but a survey published in the latest issue 
of the Lancet magazine throws up shocking statistics. 
338 

[1 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
Researchers based in Canada and India, conducted a survey among 1.1 million 
households in 1998 and studied about 1,33,738 births in 1997. According to 
this study on female foeticide by an Indo-Canadian team, about five lakh unborn 
girls-one in 25-are aborted in India every year. In 1997, projected births were 
13.6 million girls, when actual number was 13.1 million births. In 1981, Census 
reported 962 girls per 1000 boys, which got reduced to 945 in 1991 and 927 
in 2001. The imbalance is particularly ac ute in north India where the ratio has 
declined to less than 900 girls per 1000 boys. Particularly in Punjab, sex ratio has 
dwindled to 874 girls per 1000 boys.

aborting the female foetus. What, however, is of import is the absence of any 
difference whatsoever in the female foeticide law, in existence for over 11 
years now. 
Reason for the practice of female foeticide is society's preference for boys 
that continues to outweigh the acceptance of the girl child as and equal asset. 
A daughter is considered an economic burden because of the money which has 
to be spent on her dowry. Human greed and growing consumerism have 
made things worse. The argum ent that it is better to kill girl in the womb than 
see her killed for dowry is outrageous. 
While changing community's attitude is important, the problem is too 
important to await society's enlightenment. There is urgent need for the Central 
and State Governments to act with greater vigour to implement the law with the 
focus on the medical fraternity. I would also appeal to the conscience of this 
august House to rise to the occasion and to direct and urge the Government 
and the society to take steps on war-footing to curb and stop this fiendish 
murder in the womb of unborn girls.

SHRI B.S. GNANADESIKAN (Tamil Nadu):  Sir, in the Indian Penal Code, 
there is no specific offence requiring stringent punishment regarding sexual assault 
on children. The Child Marriage Restraint Act has remained only on papers as

action. Due to inbuilt problems of limited perspective and insensitive procedure, 
the existing laws did not really provide any relief to a child who had been sexually 
abused. Chief Justice of Madras High Court stressed the need to establish 
Special Courts to exclusively deal with cases of child abuse and exploitation.

where there is a reasonable apprehension that a child is vulnerable and likely to

the victim. The legal notion of sexual abuse of children is outdated. The children 
are employed even in hazardous i ndustries with labour inspectors remaining a 
passive spectator. A child of today is a proud citizen of tomorrow's india, and 
needs all care, comfort, free education, and, over and above this, our psychological 
support. Hence, I request that a suitable legislation or amendments may be 
brought in. (Ends)

Lack of Maintenance of Libraries and Reading Rooms in Orissa 
DR. RADHAKANT NAYAK (Orissa): Sir, with MPLAD funds at my disposal, 
I have started a movement of rural libraries and reading rooms in the State of 
Orissa, in which some officers are taking keen interest. Except in a few State 
and district levels, the general condition of public libraries especially in rural 
areas of the State is deplorable. Funds do not seem to be a constraint in this 
regard, since the Finance Commission has generously given its award for 
libraries and reading rooms. There is no separate Directorate, nor trained 
manpower to monitor the programme. It is feared that the Prime Minister's main 
idea of Knowledge Centres would fail in the process. 
In this background, I would urge the Central Government to bring these facts to 
the notice of Orissa Government for effective and prompt action to ensure that a 
good network of libraries and reading rooms are established for inculcating 
reading habits among the people and consequent spread of education in the 
rural areas of the State. 
Need for Mandatory Tests of HIV/AIDS before Marriage 
SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, 
thank you for giving me this opportunity. My special Mention is regarding compulsory 
tests of HIV/AIDS before marriages. Our country is on the verge of having the 
greatest increase in the estimated number of people living with HIV/AIDS in the 
world in the coming decades. The Government should adequately meet the 
challenge to scale-up the HIV/AIDS response to meet the potential increase in the 
epidemic in the coming years. These challenges include an adequate health 
workforce, responsive infrastructure, including laboratory capabilities, comprehensive 
monitoring, adequate and sustainable financing. The Government should 
consider the experience of other countries in the region that have had success in 
controlling these epidemics. The Government should highlight some key health 
system constraints that face India in its attempt to alleviate the suffering of those 
living with HIV/AIDS by 2007. 
A recent report also suggested that HIV prevalence of over 1 per cent has 
been found in pregnant women in four States, namely Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, 
Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra, and in the north-eastern States also. 
348 

[1 March, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
The HIV infection rate among pregnant women tested at antenatal clinics in 
Andhra Pradesh has been consistently above 1 per cent, which is a benchmark 
for categorizing a State as high prevalent. Wives of truck and taxi drivers showed 
higher vulnerability with 2.94 per cent of HIV positive women visiting antenatal 
clinics falling in this category. 
I request that the Government should come out with a legislation to 
mandate HIV/AIDS tests before the marriages in each State so that we can 
stop this epidemic at the budding stage, at least, to free the next generation 
from its clutches. This legislation should give more powers to act swiftly and on a 
war-footing basis. Thank you.

Problems being Faced by Handloom Weavers of Varanasi 
and Gorakhpur 
SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI (Chhattisgarh): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I 
want to draw the attention of the House to the pitiable condition of handloom 
weavers of Varanasi and Gorakhpur. The traditional silk industries of these cities were 
already facing problems and challenges thrown by liberalisation of trade. But 
the dumping of cheap silk and silk-woven garments from China further 
aggravated this problem. Due to this, 70—80 per cent of handlooms have been 
virtually closed down and the weavers are either committing suicide or migrating 
to other States. 
However, irrespective of the policies, projects and aspirations arising out of 
various quarters, the handloom sector is undergoing changes which are 
impactfng the livelihood of handloom we avers. All the schemes implemented 
through cooperatives, etc., have proved to be ineffective and before this 
traditional industry becomes extinct, I request the Government to take 
immediate maeasures like establishing relative low-cost, decentralized spinning 
units in the villages, design improvements, wider market network, patenting 
designs or varieties, protection from  unfair competition from mills and 
powerlooms, enhanced Budget allocations for the handloom sector and
